# About

URL: https://kompositenews.com/about/

About Komposite News
Komposite News is an independent digital publication covering artificial intelligence, blockchain, digital assets, enterprise technology, cybersecurity, fintech and capital markets. We write for executives, founders, investors, developers and policy professionals who need to understand how technology and finance are changing each other.
Our coverage prioritizes reporting and analysis over hype. We are interested in what is being built, what it costs, who is buying it and what the consequences are, and we hold breathless claims from any direction to the same standard of evidence.
Komposite News is edited by Cory Chamberlain, chief editor, and Noam Krasniansky, co-editor and chief content officer.
Ownership and funding: Komposite News is independently operated. Any commercial relationship relevant to a story is disclosed within that story, and sponsored content is always clearly labeled. Questions about the publication can be directed through our contact page.

# Editorial Standards

URL: https://kompositenews.com/editorial-standards/

Editorial Standards
Komposite News reports facts we can verify and clearly distinguishes reporting from analysis and opinion. News stories describe what happened. Pieces labeled Analysis interpret events and draw conclusions from evidence. Pieces labeled Opinion argue a point of view and represent their author.
We attribute information to sources wherever possible, grant anonymity only when information is significant and cannot otherwise be obtained, and independently verify claims before publishing them. We do not accept payment for editorial coverage, and staff may not trade on non-public information obtained through reporting.
Sponsored or partner content, when it appears, is labeled unambiguously and is never presented in editorial form without that label. Errors, when they occur, are corrected promptly and transparently under our corrections policy.
How we use AI
Komposite News uses AI tools to help research, draft and edit stories. Every story is checked against the sources listed with it before publication, and quotes are published only when we can match them to a source or the person approved them. An editor approves each story before it goes live. Bylines name the desk or house byline responsible for a story; they are not always individual reporters. Corrections: contact the newsroom via our contact page with the article link and the specific claim at issue, as set out in our corrections policy.

# AI Policy

URL: https://kompositenews.com/ai-policy/

AI Policy
Komposite News uses AI tools to help research, draft and edit stories, and to assist with translation and site infrastructure. AI is not a replacement for editorial judgment: every story is checked against the sources listed with it, and an editor approves each story before it goes live. Responsibility for accuracy rests with the newsroom, not with any tool used to produce it. Bylines name the desk or house byline responsible for a story; they are not always individual reporters. The full statement is in How we use AI.
Quotes are published only when we can match them to a source or the person approved them. We do not publish AI-generated statements attributed to real people, AI-fabricated data, or synthetic imagery presented as photography. Illustrations are labeled as illustrations, photographs carry credits and licenses, and sample or demonstration data is labeled as such wherever it appears.
This policy will evolve with the technology. Questions about how a specific story was produced can be directed to the newsroom via our contact page.

# What buyers actually do with an SBOM

URL: https://kompositenews.com/cybersecurity/sbom-what-buyers-do-with-it/
Section: Cybersecurity
By: Sam Porter
Published: 2026-08-30T09:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-08-30T09:00:00Z

Software bills of materials are now routinely produced and routinely ignored, and the gap between generating one and acting on it is where the risk sits.

The argument about whether vendors should produce a software bill of materials is over. Vendors produce them. The interesting question, and the one procurement teams are least prepared for, is what happens to the file after it arrives.
An SBOM is an inventory: the components inside a piece of software, their versions, and their relationships to one another. Its value is entirely conditional. It answers one question well, which is whether a newly disclosed vulnerability is present in something already installed, and it answers that question only if somebody is holding it when the disclosure lands.
The baseline moved this year. American authorities published an updated set of minimum elements, replacing guidance that had stood since the original executive order and raising what a compliant document is expected to contain.
That update matters more than it sounds, because the minimum elements are what contracts point at. A purchase order rarely specifies a format in detail. It references a standard, and the standard quietly determines how much work a vendor has to do.
Adoption across the European market has been surveyed rather than assumed. The EU cybersecurity agency's review of where SBOM practice actually stands describes an ecosystem where generation is increasingly routine and consumption remains the weak link.
That asymmetry is the whole story. Producing an SBOM is a build-pipeline problem, and build pipelines are the part of software organizations most amenable to automation. Consuming one is an operations problem, and operations teams are already the most oversubscribed function in most security programs.
The result is a familiar organizational pattern. A file arrives, satisfies a contractual requirement, and is stored where nothing queries it. The obligation is met and the risk is unchanged, which is the worst of both outcomes because it also produces a record showing the buyer was told.
Teams that get value from the practice describe the same prerequisite, and it is not tooling. It is knowing what software they run, at which version, in which environment, well enough to join that list against an inventory. Organizations that cannot answer the first question gain nothing from the second.
Regulatory drivers keep expanding the population who must care. Medical device guidance, the European cyber resilience regime and federal procurement terms each require the artifact in their own context, and each has a different theory of what the recipient is supposed to do with it.
Practitioners are candid that the honest use case is narrower than the marketing. When a widely used component is found to be catastrophically vulnerable, an SBOM turns a week of frantic archaeology into a database query. Between those events it is a maintenance cost.
That is a reasonable trade and a smaller claim than the one usually made for it. The organizations doing this well are not the ones with the best-formatted files. They are the ones who can answer, on the afternoon the disclosure lands, where the affected component is running.

# What an attestation must prove

URL: https://kompositenews.com/crypto/what-an-attestation-must-prove/
Section: Crypto
By: Marcus Oyelaran
Published: 2026-09-03T14:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-09-03T14:00:00Z

Stablecoin law requires monthly examination of reserves, and the open rulemaking question is what level of assurance that examination must actually deliver.

The argument about whether stablecoin issuers should publish their reserves is finished. Federal law requires it. The argument that replaced it is narrower, more technical, and determines whether the requirement means very much: what an examination of those reserves has to establish.
The statute sets the frame. The GENIUS Act requires permitted issuers to publish the composition of their reserves monthly, to have those reports examined by a registered public accounting firm, and to obtain certifications from the chief executive and chief financial officer.
Monthly is a demanding cadence for anything an accounting firm signs. Most public company reporting is quarterly with a single annual audit, so the law is asking for a recurring procedure that has no exact precedent at this frequency.
The open question is the assurance level, and it is not a technicality. An examination performed at limited assurance concludes that nothing came to the practitioner's attention suggesting a problem. One performed at reasonable assurance states positively that the reserves are what the issuer says they are.
Those are different products with different costs and very different meanings to a reader, and the same document title can describe either. A holder comparing two issuers' monthly reports has no reliable way to tell which standard produced them without reading the fine print.
Regulators are consulting rather than assuming. Rulemaking has asked directly whether the examination should be conducted at reasonable assurance, under established attestation standards, or under an alternative framework built for the purpose.
The content of the disclosure is comparatively settled. The expected reporting covers the par value of coins outstanding, the fair value of reserve assets by category, the weighted average maturity of Treasury holdings, the names of custodians and depository institutions, and a reconciliation showing reserves at least equal outstanding coins.
That reconciliation is the heart of it. Everything else describes the portfolio; the reconciliation is the statement that the portfolio covers the liability, and it is the sentence a holder is actually relying on when they treat a token as a dollar.
Supervisors have published implementation requirements through the ordinary rulemaking process, including standards for insured depository institutions and supervised issuers, which is how a novel instrument gets absorbed into an existing supervisory apparatus.
The practical effect of a strong answer would be consolidation. A monthly reasonable-assurance examination is expensive, requires reserve assets an accounting firm can verify quickly, and is easiest for issuers holding short Treasuries at large custodians, which is a narrower field than the one that exists today.
That may be the intended outcome. A payment instrument that circulates as a dollar substitute is a poor place for structural creativity, and the assurance standard is the lever that decides how much of it survives.

# What a seed round now requires

URL: https://kompositenews.com/startups/what-a-seed-round-now-requires/
Section: Startups
By: Grace Lindqvist
Published: 2026-08-27T09:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-08-27T09:00:00Z

Seed rounds now arrive after revenue and retention evidence that once belonged to Series A, and the gap between rounds has stretched past two years.

The seed round kept its name and quietly changed its meaning. What investors now expect before writing that check is roughly what a Series A required a few years ago, and founders planning against the old definition run out of money at the point they expected to raise.
The clearest expression of the shift is time. Data assembled from company cap tables shows the interval between rounds stretching well past two years, which means a seed round is no longer bridging to a nearby milestone. It has to fund the company to a materially different business.
That arithmetic changes how much to raise and what to promise. A round sized for eighteen months against a market that now takes twenty-four produces a company that is technically alive and practically unfundable, holding a deck full of progress and a bank balance that ends the conversation.
Investors describe the bar in terms of evidence rather than vision. Revenue that recurs, retention that survives a renewal cycle, and unit economics the founder can explain without a chart have replaced the narrative rounds that characterized the last cycle.
Pre-seed absorbed the difference. What used to be called seed is now a distinct earlier stage with its own norms and its own investors, which means the ladder gained a rung rather than losing one, and the founder climbs the same distance in more steps.
Formation costs falling has made this possible without making it pleasant. Building a credible product is cheaper than it has ever been, so the evidence investors demand is now genuinely obtainable before a round, which is precisely why it is demanded.
The concentration of capital into a narrow band of companies compounds the effect. When most of a fund's deployment goes to a small number of category-defining bets, the diligence applied to everything else tightens, because those checks have to clear a higher internal bar to justify the attention.
Founders who have raised recently describe the practical adaptation as unglamorous. Charge earlier than feels comfortable, treat the first ten paying customers as the fundraise rather than as a precursor to it, and keep the burn low enough that the round is optional for a quarter longer than planned.
The uncomfortable part is what this selects for. Requiring commercial evidence before capital favors founders who can survive unpaid for longer, which is a filter on personal circumstances as much as on ability, and the industry has not found a good answer to that.
Investors are candid that the discipline is real and its distribution is not. The companies that clear the new bar are unquestionably stronger at the same stage than their predecessors, and some number of good companies never got far enough to be measured.
The stage will keep its name regardless. It is worth understanding that the word now describes a company with customers, and planning the eighteen months before it accordingly.

# AI in the order flow: what machine trading is doing to volatility

URL: https://kompositenews.com/markets/volatility-market-structure-ai-trading/
Section: Markets
By: Priya Raghavan
Published: 2026-07-17T15:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-07-17T15:00:00Z

Adaptive execution and model-driven strategies are changing intraday dynamics in ways researchers are only beginning to measure.

Machine learning has been in markets for years, but the current generation of adaptive execution and model-driven strategies behaves differently from its rule-based ancestors, and researchers are working out what that means for volatility itself.
Early findings are mixed in instructive ways. Adaptive strategies appear to dampen volatility in normal conditions, adjusting quickly to absorb flow imbalances, while contributing to sharper moves when many models respond to the same signal simultaneously. Calm most days, and a faster crowd on the days that matter.
Regulators are asking measurement questions before policy ones: how much flow is model-driven, how correlated are the models, and whether existing circuit breakers match the speed of the herding they are meant to interrupt. Exchanges, holding the data, have become reluctant referees in the debate.
RelatedDigital asset market making becomes an institutional business ›Practitioners mostly shrug at the framing. Every generation of market technology, they note, was accused of breaking volatility until it became the baseline against which the next generation was accused. The honest answer is that the market is running the experiment on itself, and the results publish in real time.

# Machine identity sprawl becomes security's biggest inventory problem

URL: https://kompositenews.com/cybersecurity/identity-machine-workloads/
Section: Cybersecurity
By: Sam Porter
Published: 2026-07-10T10:55:00Z
Updated: 2026-07-10T10:55:00Z

Service accounts, API keys, and agent credentials now outnumber human identities many times over, and governance is racing the growth.

For every human identity in a modern enterprise there are many machine ones, service accounts, API keys, certificates, and now AI agent credentials, and most organizations cannot count them, let alone govern them. Machine identity has become the inventory problem that defines the next phase of identity security.
The risk profile is distinctive: machine credentials are long-lived, widely copied, and rarely owned by anyone who remembers creating them. Incident reviews repeatedly trace breaches to forgotten service accounts with standing privileges, and the remediation is lifecycle discipline, issuance, rotation, expiry, applied at a scale human identity never required.
RelatedCybersecurity spending shifts toward identity and resilience ›Agentic AI raised the stakes by adding credentials that act autonomously. The emerging standard treats every agent as a governed identity with scoped permissions and an accountable human sponsor, which is less a new idea than the old one, finally enforced on the population that grew fastest.

# Enterprises write the rulebook for AI-generated code

URL: https://kompositenews.com/ai/ai-coding-tools-enterprise-standards/
Section: AI
By: Tom Kessler
Published: 2026-06-26T13:30:00Z
Updated: 2026-06-26T13:30:00Z

Provenance tracking, review gates, and dependency policies are turning AI coding assistance from a developer perk into governed infrastructure.

AI coding assistants arrived in enterprises through developer enthusiasm and settled in ahead of policy. The policy is now catching up. Engineering organizations are formalizing rules for machine-generated code: what must be tracked, what must be reviewed differently, and what may not be generated at all.
Provenance is the anchor requirement. Compliance teams want to know which code a model wrote, which model wrote it, and what the model was shown, both for license exposure and for the audits that regulated industries already face. Tooling vendors have responded with attribution tracking that engineering leaders describe as necessary and nobody describes as finished.
RelatedAI infrastructure spending moves into a new phase ›The practical effect on productivity has been smaller than skeptics predicted. Teams report that governance slowed adoption for a quarter and then became routine, the same arc that source control and code review followed in earlier decades. The tools stayed; the anarchy did not.

# AI evaluation grows from afterthought to budget line

URL: https://kompositenews.com/ai/ai-evaluation-becomes-budget-line/
Section: AI
By: Dana Whitfield
Published: 2026-08-05T13:40:00Z
Updated: 2026-08-05T13:40:00Z

Enterprises deploying models at scale are formalizing evaluation the way they once formalized QA, and a vendor category is forming around it.

When AI systems were pilots, evaluation was a spreadsheet. Now that they process claims, answer customers, and draft contracts, companies are treating evaluation as standing infrastructure, with dedicated staff, tooling budgets, and sign-off authority over releases.
The change is driven less by regulation than by incident reports. Organizations that shipped model updates without regression testing describe the same experience: a quiet degradation in some workflow no one was watching, discovered by customers rather than dashboards. Formal evaluation pipelines are the institutional response.
A market is forming to serve the need. Startups sell evaluation harnesses, scored datasets tailored to industries, and monitoring that flags drift in production. Incumbent observability vendors are extending into the category, arguing that model behavior is simply another production signal.
RelatedEnterprise buyers push for clearer AI contract terms ›The maturity marker executives cite is procedural: whether a model change can be blocked. In organizations where evaluation owns a veto, the function is real. Where it produces reports no one must read, it remains a spreadsheet with a bigger budget.

# Power availability becomes the master constraint on computing

URL: https://kompositenews.com/technology/power-constraints-shape-computing/
Section: Technology
By: Jonathan Bright
Published: 2026-07-27T09:15:00Z
Updated: 2026-07-27T09:15:00Z

Grid interconnection queues, not chip supply, now set the timeline for new capacity, and the industry is reorganizing around electrons.

Ask data center developers what gates their next project and the answer is no longer silicon. It is the interconnection queue, the multi-year wait for utility approval to draw large amounts of power from grids that were not planned for computing's growth curve.
The constraint is reorganizing the industry's geography and structure. Development migrates to regions with spare generation and faster approvals; operators contract directly for new generation, sometimes co-developing it; and a market has emerged in sites whose chief asset is a signed interconnection agreement.
On-site and adjacent generation has moved from contingency to strategy. Gas turbines as bridge power, long-term contracts anchoring new renewable buildouts, and serious capital behind small modular nuclear all reflect the same conclusion: waiting for the grid is the expensive option.
RelatedLiquid cooling stops being optional in AI data centers ›The policy dimension is unavoidable. Computing's power demand lands on ratepayers, regulators, and climate commitments simultaneously, and jurisdictions are diverging on who pays for the upgrades and who gets priority in the queue. Where those questions get answered favorably is, increasingly, where the next generation of infrastructure gets built.

# Shadow AI becomes the new shadow IT

URL: https://kompositenews.com/business/shadow-ai-governance-problem/
Section: Business
By: Sam Porter
Published: 2026-08-07T11:25:00Z
Updated: 2026-08-07T11:25:00Z

Employees are routing work through unsanctioned AI tools faster than policies can name them, and enterprises are choosing between control and visibility.

Every technology wave produces its shadow, and AI's arrived on schedule. Employees across functions are routing drafting, analysis, and coding through personal accounts on consumer AI tools, outside procurement, outside logging, and outside whatever policy the company wrote last quarter.
The governance instinct is prohibition, and the operational evidence is that prohibition fails quietly. Organizations that blocked consumer tools report usage migrating to personal devices, trading visible risk for invisible risk. The emerging alternative is substitution: sanctioned tools good enough that the shadow versions lose their appeal, paired with monitoring that treats AI traffic like any other data flow.
RelatedEnterprise software pricing strains under the weight of AI ›Security leaders describe the moment in familiar terms, because they lived it with cloud storage and messaging apps. The lesson they cite from those episodes is consistent: the workforce adopts what works, and governance succeeds by arriving with a better answer rather than a longer denial.

# Instant payments become table stakes in B2B

URL: https://kompositenews.com/fintech/instant-payments-b2b-standard/
Section: Fintech
By: Elena Vasquez
Published: 2026-08-12T11:20:00Z
Updated: 2026-08-12T11:20:00Z

Real-time rails are moving from consumer novelty to supplier expectation, and the software layer on top is where the margin lives.

Instant payment rails, built for consumers splitting dinner, are being colonized by business finance. Supplier payments, insurance disbursements, and payroll adjustments increasingly ride real-time systems, and the expectation is spreading through supply chains faster than the infrastructure teams behind it anticipated.
The shift exposes where the value actually sits. Moving money instantly is becoming a commodity; knowing why it moved is not. The software that attaches invoices, remittance data, and reconciliation to real-time payments commands the margin the rails themselves are losing.
Corporate adoption follows a practical script: start with the payments where speed is worth money, urgent supplier releases, claim payouts, final payrolls, then expand as finance teams trust the controls. Fraud tooling has had to accelerate in parallel, since irrevocable and instant is a demanding combination.
RelatedWhen software spends: payments build an authorization layer for AI agents ›Banks find themselves both essential and squeezed, operating the rails while fintech intermediaries own the customer experience above them. The competitive response, embedding payment capabilities directly into the software businesses already use, is reshaping bank product organizations around a fact they long resisted: the interface is the relationship.

# Stablecoin Reserve reporting converges on common standards

URL: https://kompositenews.com/crypto/stablecoin-reserve-transparency-standards/
Section: Crypto
By: Elena Vasquez
Published: 2026-03-06T08:45:00Z
Updated: 2026-03-06T08:45:00Z

Monthly attestations are giving way to standardized disclosures that let treasurers compare issuers the way they compare money market funds.

Stablecoin issuers are learning to speak the language of money market funds. Reserve disclosures, once a patchwork of voluntary attestations in incompatible formats, are converging on standardized reporting of composition, maturity, and counterparties, driven by regulation in some jurisdictions and competitive pressure everywhere else.
The audience is corporate. Treasurers evaluating stablecoins for payments want the same visibility they get from a fund fact sheet, and issuers courting that demand have discovered that transparency is a product feature. Disclosure quality now appears in payment providers' issuer scorecards alongside redemption terms.
Standardization enables comparison, and comparison disciplines behavior. Analysts publishing side-by-side reserve breakdowns note measurable shifts toward shorter maturities and simpler holdings since standard formats took hold, the market rewarding conservatism it can finally see.
RelatedStablecoin law meets its implementation year ›Gaps remain, particularly in real-time reporting and the treatment of reserves held across borders. But the direction is set, and it points toward stablecoins being evaluated with the tools of cash management rather than the vocabulary of crypto.

# Interoperability standards take shape for institutional chains

URL: https://kompositenews.com/blockchain/interoperability-standards-institutional-chains/
Section: Blockchain
By: Jonathan Bright
Published: 2025-11-12T10:05:00Z
Updated: 2025-11-12T10:05:00Z

Messaging standards bodies and blockchain consortia are converging on formats that let regulated ledgers talk to each other, and to the systems banks already run.

The institutional blockchain world is discovering what payments learned decades ago: networks that cannot interoperate stay small. Standards work, unfashionable and slow, has become the venue where the next phase of adoption is actually being decided.
The convergence underway joins two traditions. Financial messaging bodies bring the discipline of standardized data formats that banks already parse, while blockchain consortia bring transfer protocols proven on public networks. The emerging designs let a tokenized asset move between regulated ledgers while carrying the structured information compliance systems require.
Progress is measured in pilots that would once have been impossible: assets issued on one institution's ledger settling against payment on another's, with both sides reconciled automatically. Participants emphasize that none of it required the institutions to share a chain, only a vocabulary.
RelatedBanks test blockchain settlement without abandoning existing rails ›The stakes are consolidation versus fragmentation. If common standards hold, tokenized markets can scale across institutions the way correspondent banking did. If they fail, each network remains an island, and the efficiency case for the technology weakens accordingly.

# Nvidia's board opens an inquiry, 394 days after Megaspeed

URL: https://kompositenews.com/ai/nvidia-board-opens-inquiry-394-days-after-megaspeed/
Section: AI
By: Dana Whitfield
Published: 2026-11-09T16:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-11-09T16:00:00Z

Nvidia's board opened an independent inquiry on 8 Nov into reports Jensen Huang was targeted by foreign intelligence. Our timeline and filing analysis.

Nvidia's board said on Sunday that a committee of its independent directors, with outside counsel, will investigate reports that Jensen Huang, the company's founder and chief executive, "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort". The statement names neither the directors nor the law firm, and says the board has confidence in Huang.
Its central sentence is a careful one: "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information." It does not mention Megaspeed, the Singapore-based cloud company at the centre of the reports, or Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive whom US intelligence agencies suspect of passing information to Beijing, according to reports cited by CNBC.
Huang's own email to staff, posted on Nvidia's newsroom the same day, names neither of them either. "I was unfaithful to my wife," he wrote. "My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did." CNBC reported that the affair was with Alice Huang. On the security question, the email says only that the board has begun an investigation and that he will "cooperate fully". Nvidia told CNBC: "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption."
How long have the questions been public?
More than a year. By our count, 394 days passed between the first public confirmation of an official inquiry into Megaspeed and the board's statement. On 10 October 2025, Singapore's police told CNBC that "investigations are ongoing into Megaspeed for suspected breaches of our domestic laws", after reports that the company had helped Chinese firms get around US chip export controls. Nvidia said at the time that it had visited "multiple Megaspeed sites" and that Megaspeed was "running a small commercial cloud, like many other companies throughout the world, as allowed by U.S. export control rules", CNBC reported.
When the intelligence reports about Alice Huang appeared on 29 October this year, the company's line had not changed. "The diversion allegations against this regional cloud were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year," an Nvidia spokesperson told CNBC, adding: "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know." Ten days later the board opened its inquiry. Megaspeed has said that inspections by the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, Malaysia's trade ministry and Nvidia found "no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities", CNBC reported on Monday. Singapore's government has said it did not investigate Alice Huang's alleged intelligence ties.

Komposite's timeline from the documents linked. Day counts are calendar days, counted by Komposite, back from the board's statement of 8 November 2026 or forward from Monday 9 November.What do Nvidia's accounts show about Singapore?
Less than they used to. Until the autumn of 2025, Nvidia's financial statements broke out revenue by the country where customers were billed, and Singapore was the second-largest line after the United States. In the year to January 2025 it was $23.68bn, 18 per cent of revenue, according to the 10-K. In the quarter to July 2025 it was $10.16bn, or 22 per cent. Nvidia said repeatedly that this was an invoicing address, not a destination: "Customers use Singapore to centralize invoicing while our products are almost always shipped elsewhere." In its August 2025 quarterly report, it added that over 99 per cent of export-controlled data-centre compute revenue billed to Singapore was "for orders from U.S.-based customers".

Source: Nvidia's 10-K for fiscal 2025 and 10-Q for the quarter to 27 July 2025, geographic revenue by customer billing location. The April 2025 quarter is Komposite's subtraction of the second quarter from the first-half figures. Shares are Komposite's arithmetic.Then the line went. In the quarterly report filed on 19 November 2025, 40 days after the Singapore police confirmed their inquiry, Nvidia began reporting revenue by the location of customers' headquarters instead. It explained the change in its own terms: billing locations "often reflected a customer's centralized invoicing location, even though our products were almost always shipped elsewhere", and it believed headquarters "provides a better representation of the geographic profile of our revenue". The filing does not mention Megaspeed, and we do not suggest the change was connected to it. Its effect is that a reader of the accounts can no longer see how much is invoiced through Singapore.
What changed when the old figures were restated?
Most of the Singapore revenue became American. Nvidia restates prior periods under the new method, so the same quarter can be read both ways. Comparing the July 2025 quarter as first reported with the version printed as a comparative a year later, US revenue rises by $9.43bn and Singapore's $10.16bn disappears, which fits the company's account of where its Singapore-billed customers were based. Revenue from customers headquartered in China, including Hong Kong, is also $1.22bn higher on the new basis than the China line on the old one, and "Other" is $0.86bn lower. Since the change, all customers outside the United States, Taiwan and China have accounted for between 1.3 and 2.0 per cent of revenue in each period reported, the filings show. Megaspeed is based in Singapore, so any revenue from it as a direct customer would now sit in that small line, which the filings do not break down further.

Source: Nvidia's 10-Q for the quarter to 27 July 2025 (first column) and the prior-year comparatives in its 10-Q for the quarter to 26 July 2026 (second column). Differences are Komposite's arithmetic.What happens next?
Two dates are already fixed. Nvidia reports third-quarter results on Tuesday 17 November, with a call at 2 p.m. Pacific time. The following day is the date that three Republican committee chairmen, Brian Mast of Foreign Affairs, John Moolenaar of the Select Committee on China and Rick Crawford of Intelligence, have asked Huang to brief their committees behind closed doors. Their letter of 5 November asked him to accept that date or propose another by Wednesday, and said: "It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk." Nvidia has not said whether he will attend. Democrats have pressed separately. Senator Chris Coons, in line to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee from January, wrote that "Congress will investigate and get answers", and Representative Seth Magaziner asked for the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, to testify alongside Huang, CNBC reported.
As of 09:55 Eastern time on Monday, Nvidia had filed no Form 8-K about the inquiry with the Securities and Exchange Commission, by our check of EDGAR; its most recent filing was a director's routine report of a gift of shares. The board's statement promises "further updates as appropriate" and sets no timetable. A board inquiry run by independent directors reports to the board, and nothing in the statement commits it to publishing findings.
Why it matters: Nvidia's chips are central to US export policy toward China, and its chief executive has argued for broader chip exports there. The company's defence on Megaspeed has rested for a year on its own site visits and on export rules that allow remote cloud services. Its board is now examining the same relationship from a different angle, the security of the company's own information. The export-control system has been shifting from rule-writing to enforcement through penalties and settlements, and Nvidia's role in financing its own customers has drawn questions of its own, as when it considered guaranteeing debt for chips it sells. The results on 17 November will be the first chance for analysts to ask the company about any of it.

# A Microsoft redesign that earns IREN no delay credits

URL: https://kompositenews.com/markets/a-microsoft-redesign-that-earns-iren-no-delay-credits/
Section: Markets
By: Priya Raghavan
Published: 2026-11-09T15:40:00Z
Updated: 2026-11-09T15:40:00Z

IREN's 10-Q says a Microsoft-requested network change pushes delivery dates with no delay credits. Its $4bn ARR target moves to January or February.

"At Microsoft's request, we are implementing a network design change across the Horizon deployments," IREN told investors in its quarterly report filed on Thursday. The next sentence sets the terms. Under its contract with Microsoft, "delivery dates are extended, without delay credits, for delays resulting from a Microsoft-requested change". The Nasdaq-listed company, which turned from bitcoin mining to renting out AI computing, has four 50-megawatt Horizon deployments for Microsoft at Childress, Texas.
A delay credit is a payment or discount a supplier owes when it misses a delivery date. The clause means Microsoft cannot claim one for the delay it asked for. It does not say who pays for the redesign itself. The filing says the change "is being implemented in parallel with discussions regarding delivery dates and the application and payment of fees, credits and cost reimbursements". Those discussions are not finished, and IREN does not say what it has asked for.
What has slipped?
The date for IREN's headline target. In its August results, IREN said more than $4bn of annualised run-rate revenue, or ARR, was "targeted to be operational by December 31, 2026". ARR is the company's own measure: contracted hourly GPU prices for machines in service, multiplied by the 8,760 hours in a year. Thursday's release moves the target to 31 January 2027 "following a customer-requested change and supplier timing", adding that it "may extend to February 2027". By our count that is a slip of 31 to 59 days. The 10-Q's risk factors give a third cause, saying the capacity is now expected the following quarter "as a result of a customer-requested design change, supply timing and third-party delays".
The descriptions of the Horizons have also moved. In August, Horizon 1 had been delivered, Horizon 2 was in commissioning and Horizons 3 and 4 were in late-stage construction for delivery in the fourth quarter. In November, Horizon 1 is in service and Horizons 2 to 4 are all described as in late-stage construction. Daniel Roberts, IREN's co-founder and co-chief executive, said in the release that the contracted ARR "is funded and now targeted for January, after a customer-requested design change and supplier timing moved it from year-end".
27 August 20265 November 2026
Target date for more than $4bn of ARR31 December 202631 January 2027, possibly end of February
Operating ARR$1bn (26 August)"a billion"
Horizon 2 for MicrosoftCommissioning under wayLate-stage construction
Horizons 3 and 4Late-stage construction, delivery in Q4 2026Late-stage construction
Capital commitments$13.81bn (30 June)$18.95bn (30 September)
Funding position$14bn of cash, committed financing and prepayments$9bn of the $15bn remaining FY27 capex covered; $6bn targeted
Source: IREN's FY26 results release, its Q1 FY27 results release and its 10-Q. Komposite's side-by-side comparison; ARR is IREN's own operating metric, not revenue.What does waiting cost IREN?
The filing points to at least one running cost: interest on money it cannot yet spend. A financing subsidiary arranged $3,645m for the GPUs and infrastructure at Horizons 1 to 4: a $1,545m delayed-draw term loan and $2,100m of senior secured notes sold in a US private placement at 5.96 per cent. Note proceeds sit in escrow until release conditions are met. At 30 September, $1,050m was held there, and the notes "bear interest from their respective issue dates, including while the proceeds remain in escrow". One $525m tranche was released on 1 October. By our subtraction, that leaves $525m in escrow on the filing's account. Repayments on the first tranche began in September, after Microsoft accepted Horizon 1.
The quarter itself was IREN's largest yet. Revenue rose to $228m from $137m in the June quarter, and AI Cloud revenue reached $200m, of which $65m was lease revenue that the 10-Q says includes the Microsoft contract. Bitcoin mining brought in $28m, from 402 coins mined against 2,039 a year earlier, a fall of 80 per cent by our arithmetic. The net loss was $263m. The company put its revenue backlog at $20.3bn, up 22 per cent, with about two-thirds owed by investment-grade counterparties.
Is the rest of the build-out paid for?
Not all of it. IREN says the programme behind the $4bn target is "fully funded", a term its release defines to include undrawn facilities and prepayments not yet received, subject to conditions. Its wider plan is larger. Of $15bn of capital spending it still plans for the year to June 2027, $9bn is covered by cash and committed financing and $6bn is "target" financing, subject to market conditions: 40 per cent of the remainder, by our arithmetic. Contracted capital commitments rose 37 per cent in the quarter, to $18.95bn from $13.81bn. The August figure of $14bn in cash and committed funding, less the $5.1bn the company spent on investments during the quarter, comes to about the $9bn it now reports, so the two releases agree.
Why it matters: the AI infrastructure trade rests on delivery dates. Investors in neoclouds, the specialist GPU landlords, have been pricing in more risk, as Komposite reported when CoreWeave's bond yields neared 15 per cent, and much of the sector's debt is tied to contracts with a few large tenants. IREN's filing shows how much leverage a tenant like Microsoft has inside such a contract: it can change the design, and the supplier absorbs the wait. Who pays for the redesign is still being negotiated.
The next markers are delivery dates. IREN expects the Horizons to be handed over in the coming quarter, and its January target date for the ARR is 83 days away. The company owns the land and power under its sites, a legacy of its bitcoin-mining years, and says that gives it more ways to fund growth.

# Strategy sells common stock to buy back its preferred

URL: https://kompositenews.com/crypto/strategy-sells-common-stock-to-buy-back-its-preferred/
Section: Crypto
By: Marcus Oyelaran
Published: 2026-11-09T15:20:00Z
Updated: 2026-11-09T15:20:00Z

Strategy's 9 Nov filing shows $188.3m of new-share money went to STRC buybacks and $81.9m to bitcoin. Our six-week tally: $1.16bn of buybacks.

Two dollars in three that Strategy raised from new common shares last week went to buying back its own preferred stock, its Form 8-K filed on Monday shows. The company sold 2,051,348 class A shares for net proceeds of $283.8m between 2 and 8 November. It spent $188.3m repurchasing 1,887,464 shares of its STRC preferred, $81.9m on 1,036 bitcoin and put the remaining $13.6m into cash.
Strategy, formerly MicroStrategy, describes itself as the largest institutional holder of bitcoin. It held 850,364 coins as of Sunday, bought for $64.16bn at an average of $75,456 each, fees included. Its weekly filings usually lead with bitcoin bought with new money. Lately the larger figure has been in the repurchase table. STRC, which Strategy calls Stretch, is a perpetual preferred share with a variable dividend, and the company has been buying it back every week since the end of September.
How much has gone into buybacks?
By our tally, $1.16bn in six weeks. Komposite added up the repurchase and bitcoin tables in each weekly filing from 5 October to Monday's. Strategy bought back $1,163.2m of STRC over that stretch and bought 2,698 bitcoin for $219.7m, so the buybacks were about 5.3 times the bitcoin purchases. In one week, 19 to 25 October, it bought no bitcoin at all and spent $204.9m on STRC.
Week (Strategy's reporting period)STRC bought backPaid fromBitcoin boughtUSD Cash at period end
28 Sep to 4 Oct (8-K)$176.3mUSD Cash, interest334 BTC, $28.7m$833.4m
5 to 11 Oct (release)$192.4mNot stated250 BTC, $21.5m$640.5m
12 to 18 Oct (8-K)$193.1mUSD Cash267 BTC, $22.1m$447.3m
19 to 25 Oct (8-K)$204.9mUSD CashNone$242.4m
26 Oct to 1 Nov (8-K)$208.2mUSD Cash811 BTC, $65.5m$132.7m
2 to 8 Nov (8-K)$188.3mNew MSTR shares1,036 BTC, $81.9m$146.2m
Six weeks$1,163.2m2,698 BTC, $219.7m
Komposite's tally of Strategy's weekly Forms 8-K. The first row combines the two short periods in the 5 October filing ($102.6m for 28 to 30 September and $73.7m for 1 to 4 October). The 12 October release says only that the week's bitcoin was bought with share proceeds and $0.5m of USD Cash; it does not say what paid for the STRC repurchases.Why did the source of the money change?
Because the cash pile it had been using was nearly spent. Strategy keeps two pots of dollars: a USD Reserve, which it says is meant to cover preferred dividends and interest on its debt, and "USD Cash", which management can use for wider purposes including buybacks. Until last week the STRC repurchases came out of USD Cash, which fell from $833.4m on 4 October to $132.7m on 1 November, a drop of $700.7m by our subtraction. Last week was the first in the run in which the filing says new common shares paid for them. The reserve itself has barely moved: $4.77bn on Sunday, against $4.88bn in early October.
The board has twice made room for the purchases. On 19 October, Strategy said its directors had raised the authorisation under what it calls its digital credit securities repurchase programme from $2.0bn to $3.0bn. After last week, $560.3m of that remains, so roughly $2.44bn of the $3.0bn has been used, by our arithmetic. A separate $1.0bn authorisation to buy back MSTR common stock has not been touched.
What price is Strategy paying?
Just under $100 a share, every week. Dividing each week's aggregate purchase price by the shares repurchased gives averages between $99.06 and $99.76. That matters because STRC is meant to trade near $100. In a filing on 15 October, Strategy set the STRC dividend at 12.00 per cent a year for November and said management would recommend keeping it there "until STRC has demonstrated sustained, healthy trading near $100 per share". From 1 November the dividend is declared for every calendar day. The company has not said in these filings why it is buying the shares back, and the repurchases' effect on the price is not something the filings measure.
Where does that leave the bitcoin?
Below its cost, at Monday's price. Bitcoin traded at $74,812 at 14:58 GMT, according to CoinGecko, $644 below Strategy's average purchase price. At that price, by our arithmetic, the 850,364 coins were worth about $63.62bn, some $540m less than Strategy paid. Its last three purchases cost between $79,012 and $82,900 a coin, above the average, so each recent purchase has nudged the average up by a few dollars, from $75,446 on 18 October to $75,456 now. The common shares Strategy sold last week went for an average of $138.35 net, by our division, against $139.15 the week before.
Why it matters: Strategy's model depends on selling securities to investors who want exposure to bitcoin, and its preferred shares are the part of that machine that promises a fixed-looking income. When the company sells common stock to support the price of its preferred, it is moving value between its own classes of investor rather than adding bitcoin. Holders of MSTR are absorbing the dilution, and holders of STRC are getting a buyer near par. Neither shows up in the bitcoin count. Bitcoin holders elsewhere have had their own reminders of where the price thresholds sit, as Komposite found when Bitget's user fund was measured in coins rather than dollars.
Strategy has filed these updates on Mondays, which would make the next one due on 16 November. It will show whether the buybacks continue with $560.3m of authorisation left, and whether last week's switch to new common shares was a one-off. Strategy is not the only company leaning on preferred stock this autumn: Meta sold $12.5bn of mandatory convertible preferred alongside its common stock last month, as Komposite reported. That money was raised, not spent retiring an earlier issue.

# The dealer quoted $1,270 for my Range Rover key. A locksmith charged $550

URL: https://kompositenews.com/business/range-rover-key-dealer-quote-1270-locksmith-550/
Section: Business
By: Cory Chamberlain
Published: 2026-11-05T20:22:00Z
Updated: 2026-11-05T20:22:00Z

A dealer quoted $1,270 for a replacement Range Rover key; a Pittsburgh mobile locksmith did it on-site for $550. Where the money goes, and how to vet a locksmith.

A Land Rover dealership quoted me $1,270 to replace the key to my Range Rover. LocKey Locksmith, a mobile locksmith in Pittsburgh, cut and programmed a new one in my driveway for $550. That is $720, or 57 percent, less than the dealer's price.
I paid the locksmith's bill myself, and I am reporting the numbers because few owners know a cheaper option exists until they need it. The gap between the two prices comes almost entirely from labor and programming. The key itself is cheap.
Why does a Land Rover key cost so much to replace?
Most of the price pays for programming, not for the key. Land Rover's current models, the Range Rover, Range Rover Sport, Evoque, Discovery, Discovery Sport and Defender, use keys that carry a transponder chip or work as a proximity fob. A transponder is a small chip that sends a coded signal to the car's immobilizer, the anti-theft system that stops the engine from starting without a recognised key. A cut blade with no matching code will open a door but will not start the car.
Matching a new key to the car takes diagnostic equipment and software that can talk to the vehicle's security modules. Dealers charge a premium for that work. A growing number of independent automotive locksmiths have bought comparable tools and do the same job at the car.
ItemApproximate cost
Key blank or fob shell$20 to $30
Coding the chip and programming the key to the carabout $200
Mobile service call (travel, equipment, on-site labor)about $100
Paid to LocKey Locksmith, in my driveway$550
Land Rover dealership quote$1,270
Difference$720 (57 percent less)
Component costs are typical trade prices gathered for this article, not an itemised invoice. The $550 and $1,270 figures are the author's own payment and quote for the same Range Rover key. Percentage is Komposite's arithmetic.What does the dealer's price leave out?
The dealer's quote did not include the cost of getting the car there. An owner who has lost every key cannot drive to the service department, so a tow comes first. Dealer service departments often book days ahead and may have to order the fob, and someone has to arrange rides to and from the dealership. Pittsburgh owners also have few dealers to choose between, which leaves little competition on price.
The locksmith's visit avoided all of that. The car did not move, the technician brought the cutting and programming equipment, and the job took a single service call.
What does a mobile locksmith actually do?
LocKey, which dispatches from Pittsburgh's 15217 ZIP code and operates around the clock, describes a five-step process on its website. The technician verifies that the customer owns the vehicle, cuts the blade, programs the key to the immobilizer, tests the locks, ignition and remote, and hands over the key. The firm says it gives a price before starting, and that the total depends on the key type, the model and year, how complex the programming is, and whether the call comes after hours.
The ownership check matters. A locksmith willing to program a key to a luxury SUV without confirming who owns it is also willing to do it for a thief.
How do you check a locksmith in Pennsylvania?
Pennsylvania does not license locksmiths statewide, unlike states such as New Jersey and Texas, so the checking falls to the customer. LocKey trades as LocKey LockSmith LLC and lists Pennsylvania Home Improvement Contractor registration PA175243, which can be looked up in the Attorney General's contractor search. That is a registration with the state, not a locksmith's license.
The common complaint against bad operators is a low price on the phone and a much larger bill once the car is open. Ask for the full price, including programming and the service call, before work begins, and get it in writing.
Is there a cheaper way?
Yes: replace a key before the last one is gone. "All keys lost" is the most expensive version of the job because there is no working key to copy. Adding a spare while one still works costs a fraction of that. Keeping the spare at home rather than in the car, changing the fob battery when range weakens, and keeping fobs away from water and heat all lower the odds of ending up there.
Why it matters: car keys have become small computers, and replacing one is now an electronics job priced like a repair. For owners of luxury models, the dealer is the default but not the only choice. In my case the alternative came to the driveway and cost $720 less.

# Six hundred patients and a text thread

URL: https://kompositenews.com/business/six-hundred-patients-and-a-text-thread/
Section: Business
By: Dana Whitfield
Published: 2026-11-05T19:55:00Z
Updated: 2026-11-05T19:55:00Z

An Ohio direct primary care practice caps panels at 600 and answers by text and video. What it runs on, where AI fits and how employers come in.

Patients at Maple Health can reach their care team by text, video, phone or email at any hour. Each clinician keeps no more than 600 of them, the practice's website says, against the "2,000 to 3,000 patients per clinician" it calls usual in traditional care.
The Mentor, Ohio, practice runs on direct primary care, a membership model. Patients pay a flat monthly fee, and the practice does not bill an insurer for each visit.
That model sets technology a different test. In a fee-for-service clinic, software tends to justify itself by helping a practice bill more encounters. When the fee covers the relationship, a tool earns its place only by giving clinicians time back for patients.
Dr. Richard Berry, a family physician, founded the practice in 2022 and is its owner and chief executive. He spent six years in the British Royal Marines, he says, including tours in Afghanistan and Iraq, before training at Leicester Medical School in England and completing his family medicine residency at MetroHealth in Cleveland.
Since then the practice has built its care around round-the-clock access, a small panel and a collaborative team. Direct primary care can restore "time, continuity, communication, and a stronger focus on prevention rather than simply reacting to illness," Dr. Berry said.
Members choose their clinician. Memberships with one of the practice's physician assistants run $70 to $90 a month, depending on age. Membership with Dr. Berry costs $125, according to the practice's plans page. Two new doctors join the practice in April, which Dr. Berry said will give it more than enough room to take on new patients. "Physician assistants at Maple Health manage their own patient panels within a collaborative clinical team rather than functioning simply as a way to increase visit volume," he said.
He sees a broader shift under way. "Primary care is shifting from transactions to subscriptions," he said. A membership practice, in his view, "is paid to keep a patient cared for over time, whether the work happens in the office, by phone, by message, or through proactive follow-up."
What it runs on
Maple Health's home page promises "complete 24/7 access to your care team" in the clinic and by video, voice, text and email, with same-day and next-day appointments. Its "Enroll Now" button opens a sign-up page hosted by Atlas.md, which calls itself "EMR Software for Direct Care Medicine" and offers subscription billing, self-booking, video visits and text messages filed to the patient's chart. Atlas.md was the records system most used by respondents to the American Academy of Family Physicians' 2026 direct primary care data brief, at 26 per cent.
The brief drew on 313 family physicians who had engaged with the academy's direct primary care material, a 9.3 per cent response rate. Of those, 167 were practising in the model.
Direct primary care practices202220242025
Share with employer contracts65%63%55%
Average e-visits a week71113
Average patient paneln/a402504
Practices using AI-enabled toolsn/an/a66%
Komposite analysis. The AAFP figures show care moving online. The average practice logged 13 e-visits a week in 2025, almost double the 2022 figure.
Where AI fits
Dr. Berry's test for AI is simple. "AI should increase the amount of doctor-patient interaction, not replace doctors," he said. Two in three AAFP respondents said their practices had adopted AI-enabled tools, and 49 per cent used AI for clinical purposes. His broader goal is a system "with fewer administrative barriers between patients and their clinicians," he said.
The employer market
Maple Health is expanding direct primary care to employers, an extension of the model it already runs. Its employer page offers a business membership at $90 a month per adult with a $60 joining fee, open to groups as small as two. Companies with 60 or more employees also get a physician assistant on site one full day a month. The page pairs the membership with insurance meant mainly for larger medical expenses.
Employer contracts are familiar territory nationally. In the AAFP brief, 55 per cent of practising respondents had them in 2025, down from 63 per cent in 2024. Most clients are small. Among practices with contracts, 69 per cent worked with employers of fewer than 10 people and 59 per cent with employers of 10 to 25. Twenty-two per cent had clients with more than 250 workers.
Those employers mostly want visit counts. About a quarter of practices with employer contracts said clients asked for data, and 95 per cent of those requests were for visit counts. Only 23 per cent sought quality measures. A practice whose care happens in text threads and video calls will need records that show employers that work too.
Large employers are looking for ways to manage rising costs. In Business Group on Health's 2027 employer survey of 127 companies, respondents projected a median rise of 9.2 per cent in health care costs for 2027, or 8 per cent after plan design changes, and 60 per cent said they were elevating prevention and primary care, according to the group's announcement. In last year's survey, 35 per cent said they would provide primary care at on-site health centres, InsuranceNewsNet reported.
What comes next
Dr. Berry described the access promise to DPC News in 2023. "When I say access, that means you can text, call, or email, and you'll get a response right away, around the clock," he said. Maple Health has run on individual memberships since 2022, with a small panel and a collaborative clinical team. The open question is whether that model can scale from individual memberships into employer-sponsored primary care.
For Dr. Berry, the measure of any new tool, AI included, is whether it gives that team more time with patients it already knows well.

# Nineteen of twenty-two, mostly in safe seats

URL: https://kompositenews.com/policy/ai-super-pac-candidates-won-19-of-22-general-election-races/
Section: Policy
By: Jonathan Bright
Published: 2026-11-05T15:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-11-05T15:00:00Z

By our count of FEC filings and AP results, Leading the Future's super PACs backed winners in 19 of 22 general-election races. Most went on primaries.

Candidates backed by the AI industry's largest super PAC network won 19 of the 22 general-election races it spent on, by Komposite's match of Federal Election Commission filings to Associated Press results. One lost and two were uncalled on Thursday morning. Fifteen of the 19 winners won by more than ten percentage points.
The network is built around Leading the Future, a super PAC funded by investors including the founders of Andreessen Horowitz and OpenAI's president, Greg Brockman, which passes its money to two affiliates, Think Big and American Mission. Its rival, the Public First network, whose nonprofit arm received $20m from Anthropic, spends through Jobs and Democracy PAC and Defending Our Values PAC. Both networks were set up to fight over how AI is regulated, as Komposite reported on Election Day. That story ended on a promise: once results were in, the filings would show what each side had spent per race. This is that count.
How did we count it?
We used the FEC's own data and the AP's results, and the inputs are public. On Thursday at 09:16 Eastern time we downloaded the FEC's bulk file of 24- and 48-hour independent-expenditure reports for the 2026 cycle. An independent expenditure is spending, usually on advertising, mail or texts, that calls for a candidate's election or defeat without being coordinated with any campaign. We kept the 447 unique transactions reported by the four committees that do the networks' spending, replaced amended entries with the latest version, and added them up by candidate, by whether the money supported or opposed that candidate, and by the election each filer said it was for. We then matched each general-election candidate to the AP's calls and vote shares as published in NPR's Senate and House results data, which we checked at 09:19 Eastern time.
How much of the money went to the general election?
Less than a seventh of it. The four committees had reported $59.3m of independent expenditures when we checked, and $7.9m of that, 13.3 per cent, was marked for the general election. The rest went on primaries, runoffs and special elections. The timing shows the same pattern: the Leading the Future network's general-election items are dated from 28 May to 16 October, and the Public First network's from 20 to 23 October, so neither had reported any general-election spending dated in the final ten days before the vote. The Leading the Future network put 19.5 per cent of its money into the general; the Public First network put in 4.6 per cent. The single most expensive contest for both was a primary. In New York's 12th district, Jobs and Democracy PAC spent $13.2m supporting Alex Bores, a state assemblyman, and Think Big spent $8.2m opposing him. That one race took 35.9 per cent of everything the two networks reported. Bores finished second to Micah Lasher on 23 June, with 35.0 per cent of the vote to Lasher's 39.0 per cent on unofficial counts, PoliticsNY reported.

Leading the Future and Public First themselves report no independent expenditures; they pass money to the committees named.How did the Leading the Future candidates do?
Nineteen won, one lost and two were still being counted. The network supported 22 general-election candidates and opposed none: American Mission backed 17 Republicans with $5.46m and Think Big backed five Democrats with $1.34m. By our arithmetic, $4.56m, or 67.1 per cent of its general-election money, went to candidates who won, and $1.60m, 23.6 per cent, to the one who lost: Senator Darline Graham of South Carolina, the network's largest single general-election investment, who lost to Annie Andrews by 51.1 per cent to 46.7 per cent. In Mississippi, where the network spent $494,528 for Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, the AP had not called the race; Scott Colom led her by 1,138 votes. California's 23rd district, where it spent $140,448 for Representative Jay Obernolte, was also uncalled, with Obernolte ahead. The three candidates who were not incumbents, Letlow, Andy Barr in Kentucky and Kurt Alme in Montana, all won Senate seats that their party already held.

* Incumbent, as flagged in the AP data. Spending: Komposite's sums of general-election independent expenditures in the FEC's 24- and 48-hour reports, downloaded on 5 November 2026. Results: Associated Press calls and vote shares as published in NPR's results data, checked at 09:19 Eastern time on 5 November; the candidate's share is given first. Counts were still under way.Were these competitive races?
Mostly not. Nineteen of the 22 candidates were incumbents, according to the AP's data, and 15 of the 19 winners won by more than ten points. Only seven of the 22 races were decided by fewer than ten points or remained uncalled: Louisiana's Senate race, which Julia Letlow won by 1.8 points; three House seats in Indiana and Florida that the backed Republicans held by between 5.1 and 8.6 points; and South Carolina, Mississippi and California's 23rd. Those seven took $3.34m, or 49.1 per cent of the network's general-election money, and so far show four wins, one loss and two uncalled. The other half went to the 15 candidates who won by more than ten points, in amounts of $199,000 to $351,000 each, plus $5,000 for one. A record built mostly on safe incumbents says little about whether the spending changed any result, and we do not claim that it did.
What did the Public First network do?
It spent in three general-election races, all involving Republicans, for $1.11m in total. Defending Our Values PAC supported John Cowan in Georgia's 11th district, who won, and Alex Mealer in Texas's 9th, who lost to Leticia Gutierrez. Jobs and Democracy PAC spent $599,445 opposing Representative Gabe Evans in Colorado's 8th district, who lost to Manny Rutinel. The outcome matched the network's position in two of the three races.
CandidateRaceCommitteeSpentAP resultVote share
John Cowan (R)Georgia 11thDefending Our Values PAC$256,736 to supportWon55.4% to 44.6%
Alex Mealer (R)Texas 9thDefending Our Values PAC$258,287 to supportLost to Leticia Gutierrez (D)42.4% to 57.6%
Gabe Evans (R)*Colorado 8thJobs and Democracy PAC$599,445 to opposeLost to Manny Rutinel (D)41.6% to 54.5%
* Incumbent. Sources and method as in the table above.What does the count leave out?
Three things. First, the source is the 24- and 48-hour reports, which cover independent expenditures of $10,000 or more at any time and of $1,000 or more in the last 20 days before an election. Smaller earlier items appear only in periodic reports, which is why our total for the Public First network, $24.4m, is below the $25.2m its committees had reported through September. Second, no report from these committees filed after 28 October had appeared in the FEC's data when we checked, so any later spending is missing. Third, the results are unofficial counts, and the AP had not called every race. We did not assess each candidate's position on AI, and the networks' choice of candidates is their own.
What the networks say they want is on record. Leading the Future's spokesperson, Jesse Hunt, said in January that the group planned to "back leaders who will set aside politics to establish a clear, consistent national framework", The Washington Sun reported. Brad Carson, Public First's founder and a former Democratic congressman, told the paper: "We have $50 million and 85% of the public sentiment." We found no statement from either network on the general-election results by Thursday morning.
Why it matters: the two networks were the AI industry's most direct attempt to shape who writes its rules, and their own filings show where the effort went. Most of it was spent before the autumn, in primaries such as New York's 12th, rather than on the races decided on Tuesday. In the general election, the larger network mostly backed incumbents who were already favoured. How the new Congress handles AI, including whether federal rules should override state laws such as the 31 state election deepfake laws on the books this week, is the test both networks were funded for.

# Handsets down 26 per cent, cars up 89

URL: https://kompositenews.com/technology/qualcomm-handsets-down-26-per-cent-cars-up-89/
Section: Technology
By: Tom Kessler
Published: 2026-11-05T14:40:00Z
Updated: 2026-11-05T14:40:00Z

Qualcomm's handset revenue fell 26% to $5.1bn in its fiscal Q4 2026 while automotive rose 89% to $2.0bn. Our table shows how the mix shifted.

Qualcomm's revenue from smartphone chips fell 26 per cent to $5.14bn in its fiscal fourth quarter, while its automotive revenue rose 89 per cent to $1.99bn, the company reported on Wednesday. Total revenue for the three months to 27 September fell 8.4 per cent to $10.32bn, by Komposite's arithmetic.
The San Diego chip designer reports two businesses: QCT, which sells chips, and QTL, which licenses its wireless patents. QCT revenue fell to $9.02bn from $9.82bn, and QTL to $1.30bn from $1.41bn. In its annual report filed the same day, Qualcomm said handset revenue fell for the year mainly because of lower chipset shipments to certain major phone makers, which were reducing inventory after memory supply constraints and price rises. Automotive gained from higher revenue per unit as the product mix improved, and from $712m of extra shipments, mostly for new vehicles using its Snapdragon digital cockpit chips. Non-GAAP net income, which excludes items such as tax adjustments, fell 28.4 per cent to $2.33bn.
QCT revenue, $mQ4 FY26Q4 FY25ChangeFY26FY25
Handsets5,1376,961&minus;26.2%24,07227,793
Automotive1,9901,053+89.0%6,0043,957
Internet of things1,8881,807+4.5%7,1326,617
Automotive and IoT combined*3,8782,860+35.6%13,13610,574
Handsets as share of QCT*57.0%70.9%64.7%72.4%
Reported figures from Qualcomm's fourth-quarter results release of 4 November 2026. * Komposite's arithmetic. Fiscal 2026 ended on 27 September. Data-centre revenue is not reported separately; it moves into QCT from the first quarter of fiscal 2027.The company's guidance rests on the businesses that are not phones. "Fiscal 2027 marks the start of our non-handset revenue inflection, including the ramp of our Data Center business," said Cristiano Amon, Qualcomm's chief executive, adding that non-handset revenue was projected to grow by more than 60 per cent and that the company was "reiterating our fiscal 2027 Data Center revenue target of $5B." The release names a "multi-generational product collaboration with Amazon for AI data centers" but gives no terms. If "non-handset" means automotive, internet of things and data centre within QCT, which is our reading rather than the company's definition, growth of 60 per cent on fiscal 2026's $13.1bn would mean more than $21.0bn. Take out the $5bn data-centre target and automotive and IoT would need to grow by about 22 per cent, by our arithmetic.
The handset business has a known gap ahead. Apple and Samsung each accounted for 10 per cent or more of Qualcomm's revenue in fiscal 2026, the annual report says, and Qualcomm expects that Apple "will primarily use its own internally developed modem products" rather than Qualcomm's. The results release also lists renewed long-term patent licence agreements with Apple, Huawei and Transsion, without terms. Qualcomm said it is raising prices to reflect higher costs for wafers, packaging, memory and other inputs, with the full benefit expected in chip gross margins in the second half of fiscal 2027.
For the first quarter of fiscal 2027, Qualcomm forecast revenue of $10.4bn to $11.2bn, a midpoint of $10.8bn, with QCT at $9.0bn to $9.6bn including data centre, and non-GAAP earnings of $2.15 to $2.35 a share. For the full year it reported revenue of $43.12bn, down 2.6 per cent, and GAAP net income of $13.63bn, which includes a $5.7bn tax benefit from releasing a valuation allowance. It returned $11.67bn to shareholders through buybacks and dividends, 103 per cent of its non-GAAP net income, by our arithmetic.
Why it matters: Qualcomm is trying to replace phone revenue it expects to lose with revenue from cars and AI data centres, and this quarter showed both halves of that move at once. The memory squeeze it cites is the other side of the AI memory demand behind Samsung's record quarter, in which analysts estimated its own phone business lost money. The data-centre target puts Qualcomm in a crowded field of companies selling chips and networking for AI, alongside deals such as Marvell's agreement to buy Lumentum this week.

# Take out the token sale and Circle stood still

URL: https://kompositenews.com/crypto/circle-q3-take-out-the-token-sale-and-circle-stood-still/
Section: Crypto
By: Marcus Oyelaran
Published: 2026-11-05T14:20:00Z
Updated: 2026-11-05T14:20:00Z

Circle's Q3 2026 revenue less distribution costs rose 55% to $453m, helped by a $182m ARC token presale. Without it, by our arithmetic, it fell 7%.

Circle Internet Group, the USDC stablecoin issuer, said on Wednesday that third-quarter revenue less distribution costs rose 55 per cent to $453m, but $182m of its revenue came from the presale of its ARC network token. Strip that sale out and, by Komposite's arithmetic, the measure fell 7 per cent.
A stablecoin is a crypto token meant to hold a fixed value, in USDC's case one dollar, backed by reserves that earn interest. Circle keeps that interest as reserve income and pays part of it to distribution partners. Revenue less distribution costs, which Circle abbreviates as RLDC, is what remains after those payments and other transaction costs, and the company reports it alongside its results. Total revenue and reserve income rose 17 per cent to $865m. Reserve income, the interest itself, fell 8 per cent to $658m, which Circle attributed mainly to a 61 basis point fall in the rate it earns on reserves, now 3.5 per cent. Other revenue rose 627 per cent to $207m, "from the ARC token presale ($182 million)", the release said.
The presale was announced in May. Circle sold 740m ARC tokens at $0.30 each, raising $222m in a private placement led by a16z Crypto, with BlackRock, Apollo Funds and ARK Invest in the consortium, Cointelegraph reported at the time. That valued the network's 10bn-token supply at $3bn. Arc, Circle's own blockchain for stablecoin payments, launched its public main network on 16 September, according to the results release. By our arithmetic, Circle has now recognised 82 per cent of the presale as revenue, leaving about $40m. The release does not say how the sale is accounted for or whether any distribution cost applies to it, so our adjusted figures assume none does.
$m, third quarter2026 as reported2026 without ARC presale*2025
Reserve income658658711

Distribution and transaction costs409409447

USDC in circulation, quarter end$73.9bn$73.9bnabout $73.9bn (no change)
Reported figures from Circle's third-quarter results release of 4 November 2026. * Komposite's arithmetic: the $182m of presale revenue the company identified is removed from other revenue, total revenue and RLDC, on the assumption that no distribution cost applies to it. Margins are our calculation from the rounded figures; Circle reported 52 and 39 per cent.The underlying business grew more slowly than the headline. USDC in circulation was $73.9bn at the end of September, unchanged from a year earlier, while the average over the quarter was $73.3bn, up 8 per cent. Distribution and transaction costs fell 8.5 per cent to $409m, by our arithmetic. Net income from continuing operations rose 5 per cent to $226m, and adjusted EBITDA, on a new definition the company introduced, rose 85 per cent to $317m. The company's numbers are its own; adjusted EBITDA and RLDC are not measures defined by accounting standards.
Activity on the network grew faster than the money held on it. USDC on-chain transaction volume was $13.9tn in the quarter, up 49 per cent, and Circle's payments network, CPN, reached $41.3bn of annualised payment volume, the company said. It has agreed to buy Tazapay, a Singapore-based cross-border business payments platform, with completion expected in 2027 subject to regulatory approval. "In Q3, we saw continued proof that institutions are building and expanding on USDC," said Jeremy Allaire, Circle's co-founder, chief executive and chairman.
Circle left its full-year guidance unchanged: other revenue of $310m to $330m including recognised presale revenue, an RLDC margin of 41.7 to 43.7 per cent, and adjusted operating expenses of $570m to $585m. The margin guidance is lower than the third quarter's reported 52 per cent, which is consistent with the presale being a one-off lift rather than a new level. Circle did not say how much presale revenue remains to be recognised in the fourth quarter.
Why it matters: Circle's earnings move with two things it does not control, interest rates and the amount of USDC that customers choose to hold. With the reserve rate lower and circulation flat over a year, a one-off token sale did the work this quarter. The company is meanwhile pressing into new markets: Komposite reported last month that Circle wants to enter about 40 more countries, and that USDC had become the EU's first significant token under its crypto rules.
